description: Dear Earth Postcards is Gregorio Guirado, from São Paulo, Brazil: a 3D animation and visual effects artist with clients in 9 countries. He was VFX supervisor on the animated feature My Grandfather Is a Nihonjin (Annecy), where 3D shadow gives each 2D shot its time of day, and presented an automated Blender pipeline at Blender Conference 2025. Dear Earth follows the same ideas: the real Sun is the light, and one row of NASA data makes one postcard. Solo team, not recruiting.
summary: Dear Earth is a free postcard book in which the machines NASA left behind write home to the kids of Earth. Six machines send one postcard each: Apollo 11's Eagle, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Pioneer 10. The front is a real NASA picture, from Eagle seen from lunar orbit to the first photograph ever taken on the surface of Mars and InSight's final dusty selfie. The back is a short letter in the machine's voice for readers aged 8 to 13, beside a stamped Mission Record with the facts from NASA's NSSDCA catalog, each one linked to its source. Sunlight is the thread: Spirit, Opportunity and InSight ran on it, while Viking 1 and Pioneer 10 carried nuclear power. Sunlight decided how three of them ended: Spirit got stuck in sand and could not tilt its panels toward the winter Sun, a planet-wide dust storm silenced Opportunity, and dust on its panels silenced InSight. The Sunlight Check page asks "If it still worked, could it work right now?" and gives the height of the real Sun over every site, computed with NASA JPL Horizons. The book reads on a phone and prints for any classroom.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Dear Earth turns NASA's retired hardware into pen pals. Six machines send one postcard each: Eagle (Apollo 11), Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Pioneer 10. The book is an 18-page PDF that opens on a phone with no login and prints on ordinary A4 paper. The project link opens a public Google Drive folder: Dear-Earth-postcard-book.pdf is the book, Dear-Earth-demo-7-slides.pdf is the demo, and data-and-scripts holds the data, the scripts and the six letters.

- Front: a public NASA image, with its NASA ID and credit. Eagle seen from lunar orbit, with the laser mirror and the moonquake detector marked beside it; the first photograph ever taken on the surface of Mars, by Viking 1, with its footpad in the corner; Spirit's view from Troy, the soft soil that held it; the last image Opportunity sent home, dark with dust; InSight's final selfie, its panels covered in dust; Pioneer 10 being readied for launch in 1972.

- Back: a letter in the machine's voice, beside a Mission Record stamp: Launched, Landed, Where it rests, Powered by, Why it went quiet, What it found, Source. Every figure links to its NASA page.

After the six postcards comes the Sunlight Check: "If it still worked, could it work right now?" A table gives the height of the real Sun over every landing site at two moments on November 15, 2026. At 03:00 UTC the Sun had just risen over Eagle (0.5°), stood at 50.0° over Opportunity and 76.5° over nuclear Viking 1, and it was night for Spirit (-51.0°) and InSight (-76.2°). Nine hours later Mars had turned: day for Spirit (64.4°) and InSight (41.6°), night for Opportunity (-77.6°). Readers answer machine by machine, and the answer key adds what daylight alone cannot tell: a dust storm silenced Opportunity, and dust on its own panels silenced InSight. Pioneer 10 has no ground and no day: on November 15, 2026 it was 142 times Earth's average distance from the Sun, where sunlight is about 20,000 times fainter, which is why it carried nuclear power. The book ends with "Your turn", a blank postcard for the reader to write back to one machine.

Each Mission Record ends with what the machine changed. Eagle's laser mirror still measures how fast the Moon is drifting away from Earth, InSight's seismometer detected 1,319 marsquakes, and Opportunity's 45.16 km driving record stood until Perseverance passed it on October 11, 2026.

HOW IT WORKS

One row of data makes one postcard. A table built from NSSDCA and NASA mission pages holds each machine's facts and the link behind every fact, and each Mission Record is taken from its row. The Sun comes from the JPL Horizons API: the sub-solar point on the Moon and on Mars, hour by hour from November 14, 2026 to December 31, 2027 (9,912 rows per world). Standard spherical geometry turns that point into the Sun's height over each landing site. The same method finds Eagle's sunrise: between 01:45 and 02:00 UTC on November 15, 2026, the Sun rose again over Tranquility Base. The postcard fronts come from the NASA Image and Video Library. The book and the slides are laid out in HTML and printed to PDF. The 7-slide demo walks through one postcard, the six machines, the Sunlight Check and the data behind them.

ACCURACY

Every postcard keeps two voices apart: the letter is story, labeled as story; the Mission Record is data, and every figure on it links to a NASA page. The sunlight is computed, not chosen. The data-and-scripts folder, shared next to the book, holds the fact table, the scripts that ask JPL Horizons for the sub-solar points and for Pioneer 10's distance, the script that builds the Sunlight Check, and their saved output, so anyone can rerun the results. The Sunlight Check assumes smooth ground and the centre of the Sun's disc, rover values use the NSSDCA landing point, and Mars values show the Sun as seen from Earth, a few minutes behind. Each rover card gives the distance it drove after landing. Every picture is NASA's own image, credited by its NASA ID.

WHY IT MATTERS

NSSDCA holds the full record of every machine in this book, written for specialists. Dear Earth rewrites it for a 10-year-old without losing the record: every letter is checked with the Flesch-Kincaid formula and kept at US grade 5 or below (the six letters score from grade 1.8 to 4.7), and the Mission Record beside it keeps every NASA number and its link. It is free, needs no login and reads on a phone; once printed, it needs no device at all, so a classroom without computers can use it. Text is set in Atkinson Hyperlegible, a typeface designed for low-vision readers, and every image has alt text. There are no AI-generated images.

WHAT COMES NEXT

Adding a machine means adding a row. Next come Ingenuity, Dawn at Ceres, NEAR Shoemaker on Eros and Kepler, then the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Sojourner, Phoenix, the Surveyor landers and the ALSEP stations. Portuguese and Spanish editions for public schools in Brazil and Latin America follow, and the "Your turn" postcard can become a class activity: each student adopts a machine and writes back.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

Claude (Anthropic) helped compile the fact table, write the scripts, draft the six letters from the NASA facts, draft the text of the book and the slides, and lay them out. I reviewed and edited all of it. There are no SI-generated images: every picture is a public NASA image credited by its NASA ID. The README and the book's credits say the same.

TOOLS

Python with the textstat library; JPL Horizons API; Claude (Anthropic) as SI assistant; NASA Image and Video Library; HTML and CSS printed to PDF with Playwright (headless Chromium); Google Drive.
